stem: During spring growth, a maple tree uses much of the starch stored in its trunk, but the cellulose-rich walls of its cells continue to provide structural support. Which statement best explains why this support persists?

choices.choice_text: Cellulose provides support by serving as the tree’s main energy-storage polysaccharide after the starch supply decreases.
choices.rationale: The energy-only trap confuses cellulose’s structural role with starch’s storage role. Continued wall support comes from cellulose as a building material, not from cellulose replacing an energy reserve. Fix: Match each polysaccharide to either energy storage or structural support before explaining the observation.

choices.choice_text: Cellulose is a single sugar molecule that supplies quick energy for maintaining the tree’s supporting walls.
choices.rationale: The monomer–polymer trap treats cellulose as a monosaccharide. Cellulose consists of many linked glucose units and supports walls as a polymer, rather than acting as a single quick-energy sugar. Fix: Check whether the named carbohydrate contains one sugar unit or many linked units.

choices.choice_text: Cellulose contains glucose units covalently joined into long, linear polysaccharide chains that reinforce cell walls independently of stored starch.
choices.rationale: The tree uses starch as an energy reserve, whereas cellulose serves as a structural material. Cellulose’s long polymer chains reinforce the walls, so using stored starch does not remove that reinforcement.

choices.choice_text: Cellulose consists of folded amino acid chains whose protein fibers maintain the strength of the tree’s cell walls.
choices.rationale: The protein-misclassification trap assumes that a fibrous structural material must be a protein. Cellulose is a carbohydrate built from glucose units, not a chain of amino acids. Fix: Identify the building units before classifying a structural material as a carbohydrate or protein.

stem: An experimental adhesive contains a protein made of one polypeptide chain. The protein must retain a particular folded shape for the adhesive to hold surfaces together. A polar R group forms a hydrogen bond with another R group elsewhere in the chain. Researchers replace the first amino acid with one having a nonpolar R group, without changing the number of amino acids or their peptide-bond connectivity. Which prediction best explains a possible effect on adhesion?

choices.choice_text: Unchanged peptide-bond connectivity means the primary structure is unchanged, so the protein must retain its adhesive function.
choices.rationale: Bond-integrity trap: Preserving peptide-bond connectivity does not preserve amino acid sequence when an amino acid is replaced. The changed primary structure can affect folding even though chain length stays constant. Fix: Check amino acid identities when deciding whether primary structure has changed.

choices.choice_text: Loss of the R-group hydrogen bond directly changes secondary structure, because secondary structure is defined by hydrogen bonds between R groups.
choices.rationale: Secondary–tertiary confusion: Secondary structure involves hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, whereas the specified bond connects R groups. Disrupting this R-group interaction can affect tertiary structure and adhesive function. Fix: Locate the hydrogen-bond partners before assigning a structural level.

choices.choice_text: The replacement may disrupt an R-group interaction, altering tertiary folding and weakening the protein’s adhesive function.
choices.rationale: The substituted R group can disrupt a hydrogen bond that helps maintain the protein’s three-dimensional shape. Because adhesion requires that shape, altered folding could weaken the adhesive.

choices.choice_text: Loss of the R-group hydrogen bond separates polypeptide subunits, disrupting quaternary structure and weakening adhesion.
choices.rationale: Quaternary-structure trap: A protein with only one polypeptide has no separate polypeptide subunits to pull apart. Interactions between different regions of that chain help stabilize tertiary structure instead. Fix: Determine how many polypeptides are present before predicting subunit separation.

stem: In a bacterial cell, a linear polymer chain of six monomers is lengthened when five free monomers are added to its end one at a time by dehydration synthesis. An enzyme then hydrolyzes exactly four of the bonds linking monomers in the lengthened chain, and no other bonds form or break. Compared with the moment before lengthening began, how many separate molecules come from the chain, and what is the net water change?

choices.choice_text: Five separate molecules from the chain; one water molecule released overall.
choices.rationale: Adding five monomers forms five bonds, each releasing one water molecule. Hydrolyzing four bonds consumes four water molecules and cuts the single 11-monomer chain into five pieces, so the net change is 5 − 4 = 1 water molecule released.

choices.choice_text: Five separate molecules from the chain; nine water molecules released overall.
choices.rationale: Water-total addition error: this treats both joining and cleaving as releasing water. Dehydration synthesis releases five water molecules, but hydrolysis consumes four, so the totals must be subtracted. Fix: Subtract water used by hydrolysis from water released by dehydration synthesis.

choices.choice_text: Five separate molecules from the chain; one water molecule consumed overall.
choices.rationale: Water-direction reversal: this flips which reaction releases water. Dehydration synthesis releases water and hydrolysis uses it, and five released exceeds four used, giving a net release. Fix: Write water as a product of dehydration synthesis and a reactant of hydrolysis before tallying.

choices.choice_text: Four separate molecules from the chain; one water molecule released overall.
choices.rationale: Bond-count versus fragment-count error: this sets the number of pieces equal to the number of bonds cut. Cutting one linear chain once yields two pieces, so four cuts yield five. Fix: Start at one chain and add one molecule for each bond hydrolyzed.

stem: Students are investigating the assembly of pairs of synthetic RNA strands, each 20 nucleotides long. They add an antiparallel, complementary RNA partner to a starting RNA strand and count the paired molecules formed. They want to determine whether pairing requires complementary nucleotide order rather than simply a partner containing particular quantities of each base. Which control treatment best isolates nucleotide order? All conditions remain unchanged unless a choice specifies otherwise.

choices.choice_text: Replace the partner with an RNA strand of equal length and identical base counts, but with a noncomplementary base order.
choices.rationale: This comparison preserves strand length, base composition, concentration, and nucleic acid type while changing sequence complementarity. Reduced pairing would support the conclusion that matching A–U and C–G base pairs along the strands, rather than base composition alone, enables pairing.

choices.choice_text: Replace the partner with a complementary DNA strand containing thymine instead of uracil.
choices.rationale: The nucleic-acid-type trap changes DNA versus RNA rather than removing complementarity. The DNA partner can still form complementary base pairs with the starting RNA, and its sugar also differs. Fix: Identify whether the replacement changes base matching or instead changes nucleic acid type.

choices.choice_text: Keep the complementary RNA partner but add it at three times its original concentration.
choices.rationale: The concentration trap substitutes strand amount for nucleotide order as the experimental variable. Increasing the amount leaves complementarity intact, so any pairing difference would not isolate the effect of sequence matching. Fix: Compare the partner sequences before deciding whether a treatment tests complementarity.

choices.choice_text: Test the starting RNA strand without adding any partner strand.
choices.rationale: The missing-component baseline trap removes the entire partner instead of only its complementarity. This comparison cannot distinguish a requirement for matching base order from a requirement for any second strand. Fix: Keep the partner present while changing only whether its base order is complementary.

stem: A growing cell uses nucleic acids to store and transmit genetic information and phospholipids to build membranes. Its environment supplies insufficient nitrogen and phosphorus but adequate carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and sulfur. A researcher restores nitrogen availability to normal without changing phosphorus availability. Assuming the cell has no alternative phosphorus source, which prediction best explains the effect on production of nucleic acids and phospholipids?

choices.choice_text: Nucleic acid production returns to normal, but phospholipid production remains limited because only phospholipids require phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Nitrogen-only nucleic acid trap: Recognizing nitrogen in nucleic acids does not mean phosphorus is unnecessary. Nucleic acids require both elements, so restoring only nitrogen leaves their production limited. Fix: Check every required element before predicting that a molecule’s production will recover.

choices.choice_text: Phospholipid production returns to normal, but nucleic acid production remains limited because lipids require only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.rationale: All-lipids-are-alike trap: This applies the composition of fats to phospholipids. Phospholipids contain phosphorus, so abundant carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen cannot remove their phosphorus limitation. Fix: Identify the specific lipid type before deciding which elements it requires.

choices.choice_text: Production of both nucleic acids and phospholipids returns to normal because the added nitrogen can replace phosphorus in these molecules.
choices.rationale: Element-substitution trap: Nitrogen and phosphorus are not interchangeable building materials. Adding nitrogen cannot supply the phosphorus required to construct nucleic acids and phospholipids. Fix: Match the added element to the missing element rather than total nutrient availability.

choices.choice_text: Production of both nucleic acids and phospholipids remains limited because both require phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Nucleic acids require both nitrogen and phosphorus, while phospholipids also require phosphorus. Restoring nitrogen removes one shortage but leaves a shared building material insufficient, so neither type of molecule can be produced at its normal rate.

topic_title: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding
stem:
A wildlife center compares two liquids for use in a temperature buffer for an animal enclosure. Equal masses of water and liquid R are warmed from 18°C. The table records the heat absorbed to reach each temperature; no heat escapes, and neither liquid changes phase.

Temperature reached (°C) | Heat absorbed by water (kJ) | Heat absorbed by liquid R (kJ)
18 | 0 | 0
21 | 12 | 3
24 | 24 | 6

Which statement best describes the data and explains water’s thermal behavior?

choices.choice_text: Water requires less heat for the same temperature increase, indicating a lower specific heat capacity than liquid R.
choices.rationale: Comparison reversal: The table shows water absorbing four times as much heat as liquid R for the same warming. With equal masses, greater heat absorbed per degree indicates higher, not lower, specific heat capacity. Fix: Compare the heat values within one temperature row before identifying the higher specific heat capacity.

choices.choice_text: Water requires more heat for the same temperature increase because some absorbed energy disrupts hydrogen bonds between its polar molecules.
choices.rationale: For a 6°C increase, water absorbs 24 kJ while liquid R absorbs 6 kJ, indicating water’s higher specific heat capacity. Water’s polarity enables intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whose disruption absorbs energy. This resistance to temperature change helps stabilize biological temperatures.

choices.choice_text: Water requires more heat for the same temperature increase because absorbed energy breaks covalent bonds within its molecules.
choices.rationale: Bond-type confusion: Ordinary warming does not break the covalent bonds joining oxygen and hydrogen within water molecules. The relevant energy absorption involves disrupting hydrogen bonds between separate molecules. Fix: Locate each proposed bond within a molecule or between separate molecules.

choices.choice_text: Water requires more heat for the same temperature increase because its electrically neutral molecules are nonpolar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.
choices.rationale: Neutral-means-nonpolar misconception: Having no net charge does not make water nonpolar; its charge distribution is uneven. Hydrogen bonding between its polar molecules contributes to its high specific heat capacity. Fix: Check whether charge is distributed evenly rather than relying on the molecule’s net charge.

stem:
An animal-feed supplier needs a fat that remains solid in a cool warehouse. Three candidate fats have equal-length fatty acid chains but differ in their degree of unsaturation. Testing produces the following measurements:

Fat | Average carbon–carbon double bonds per fatty acid chain | Melting temperature (°C)
Cedar | 3 | −12
Maple | 2 | 8
Pine | 0 | 48

As the average number of double bonds decreases, which statement describes the measured trend and explains its structural basis?

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature falls because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds have more kinks and pack less closely.
choices.rationale: Reversed-trend trap: The measurements show rising melting temperatures as double bonds decrease, not falling temperatures. Removing double bonds also reduces the kinks associated with unsaturation rather than adding them. Fix: Follow the rows from three double bonds to zero and compare their melting temperatures.

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds make the fats hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity-confusion trap: This identifies the temperature trend but incorrectly attributes it to attraction to water. These fats remain generally hydrophobic; differences in chain shape and packing explain the pattern. Fix: Separate the number of chain kinks from whether a fat interacts favorably with water.

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds are more unsaturated.
choices.rationale: Saturation-definition trap: This matches the measured temperature trend but reverses the meaning of unsaturation. Fewer carbon–carbon double bonds indicate less unsaturation, and chains with none are saturated. Fix: Count carbon–carbon double bonds before comparing the degree of unsaturation.

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer kinks can pack together more closely.
choices.rationale: Moving from three double bonds to zero, the measured melting temperature rises from −12°C to 48°C. Fewer double bonds mean fewer chain kinks, allowing closer packing and helping explain the higher melting temperature.

stem: Researchers develop a soybean variety that produces seed storage fats with a greater proportion of saturated fatty acids than the original variety. Both varieties store the same mass of fat, and their fatty acid chains have the same lengths. When the seeds are compared at the same temperature, which prediction best connects the altered fatty acid composition to the properties and function of the fats?

choices.choice_text: The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be less liquid but will retain their role as an energy reserve.
choices.rationale: A higher proportion of saturated fatty acids means fewer double-bond kinks, allowing closer packing and favoring a less liquid state. This structural change does not change the fats’ biological role in storing energy.

choices.choice_text: The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be more liquid but will retain their role as an energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Reversed packing effect: This prediction incorrectly associates increased saturation with looser packing. Saturated fatty acid chains lack double-bond kinks, allowing closer packing and favoring a less liquid state. Fix: Compare chain kinks and packing before predicting which fat will be more liquid.

choices.choice_text: The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be less liquid and become water-soluble, losing their role as an energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Liquid–soluble confusion: This prediction treats a change in physical state as a change in water solubility. Increasing saturation does not make storage fats hydrophilic or eliminate their energy-storage function. Fix: Assess physical state and water solubility as separate properties.

choices.choice_text: The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be less liquid and assemble into phospholipid bilayers, replacing their role as an energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Lipid-class interchangeability: This prediction gives storage fats the bilayer-forming function of phospholipids. Increasing fatty acid saturation does not transform fats into a different lipid class. Fix: Identify whether the material is fat or phospholipid before predicting its function.

stem: A protein consists of a single polypeptide and binds a small molecule in a pocket formed by its folded structure. A hydrophobic amino acid buried near the pocket is replaced with an amino acid that has a charged R group. The chain length and peptide-bond connections remain unchanged. Which prediction best connects this replacement to protein function?

choices.choice_text: Intact peptide-bond connections preserve the primary structure, so the pocket’s shape and binding ability must remain unchanged.
choices.rationale: Bond-integrity trap: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, not merely the connections holding the chain together. Replacing an amino acid changes that sequence even when chain length and peptide-bond connections are preserved. Fix: Compare amino acid identities, not just chain length or bond connections.

choices.choice_text: The replacement changes secondary structure because secondary structure is defined by R-group interactions, reducing binding to the small molecule.
choices.rationale: Secondary–tertiary confusion: Secondary structure is stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, not defined by R-group interactions. Changes in R-group interactions can alter tertiary folding and therefore the binding pocket. Fix: Identify whether the described interactions involve backbone atoms or R groups.

choices.choice_text: Altered R-group interactions may change tertiary structure and the pocket’s shape, reducing binding to the small molecule.
choices.rationale: Replacing a hydrophobic R group with a charged R group can change interactions within the protein. These changes can alter its three-dimensional folding and the binding pocket’s shape, reducing its ability to bind the small molecule.

choices.choice_text: The replacement disrupts quaternary structure by separating the protein’s polypeptide subunits, reducing binding to the small molecule.
choices.rationale: Quaternary-structure trap: Quaternary structure involves interactions between multiple polypeptides, but this protein contains only one. Its binding pocket can change through altered tertiary structure without any subunits separating. Fix: Count the polypeptide chains before attributing a change to quaternary structure.

stem: A researcher separates molecules from a sunflower seed into two purified samples: phospholipids used in membranes and nucleic acids that carry genetic information. Which prediction about phosphorus in these samples is supported by their elemental composition?

choices.choice_text: Phosphorus will be present only in the nucleic acid sample because phospholipids lack phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Trap: Overlooking phosphorus in phospholipids incorrectly excludes the membrane sample. Phospholipids include phosphorus as part of their composition, so that sample also contains it. Fix: Check the elemental requirements of each molecule type before excluding a sample.

choices.choice_text: Phosphorus will be present only in the phospholipid sample because nucleic acids contain nitrogen instead.
choices.rationale: Trap: Treating nitrogen and phosphorus requirements as mutually exclusive incorrectly substitutes one element for another. Nucleic acids require both nitrogen and phosphorus, so nitrogen's presence does not exclude phosphorus. Fix: Ask whether each molecule contains multiple required elements.

choices.choice_text: Phosphorus will be absent from both samples because biological molecules contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.rationale: Trap: Confusing the most prevalent elements with the only required elements overlooks less abundant components. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are widespread in biological molecules, but both sampled molecule types also contain phosphorus. Fix: List the required elements for each molecule rather than stopping at the most prevalent ones.

choices.choice_text: Phosphorus will be present in both samples because it is a component of both molecule types.
choices.rationale: Building membrane phospholipids and information-carrying nucleic acids requires phosphorus as part of their composition. Separating these molecules into purified samples therefore does not eliminate phosphorus from either sample.

stem: Researchers maintain harvested potato tuber tissue with a steady supply of glucose. A treatment selectively prevents glucose monomers from being joined into starch, but glucose availability and cellulose assembly remain unchanged. Compared with untreated tissue, which outcome is best supported?

choices.choice_text: The treated tissue will accumulate less starch for energy storage, while its cellulose-based structural support remains largely unaffected.
choices.rationale: Blocking starch assembly reduces the formation of an energy-storage polysaccharide. Cellulose provides structural support, and its assembly is unaffected, so the treatment does not directly disrupt that function.

choices.choice_text: The treated tissue will lose structural support because starch is the principal polysaccharide that strengthens plant cell walls.
choices.rationale: Cellulose–starch role confusion assigns the structural function to the storage polymer. Cellulose supports plant cell walls, whereas starch stores energy; cellulose assembly continues in this tissue. Fix: Label each named polysaccharide as storage or structural before predicting the treatment's effects.

choices.choice_text: The treated tissue will maintain normal carbohydrate energy storage because cellulose can replace starch wherever glucose polymers are needed.
choices.rationale: The same-monomer, same-function misconception treats glucose polymers as interchangeable. Their organization gives them different functions, so cellulose does not replace starch as the tissue's energy-storage polysaccharide. Fix: Check whether the replacement polymer has the required function, not merely the same monomer.

choices.choice_text: The treated tissue will lack glucose for immediate energy use because blocking starch assembly prevents glucose from being produced.
choices.rationale: Polymer-assembly versus monomer-production confusion mistakes joining glucose units for making glucose. The treatment blocks starch formation, while the stem explicitly preserves glucose availability. Fix: Separate monomer availability from polymer assembly, then identify which process the treatment changes.

stem: A researcher asks whether phosphorus availability limits cells’ production of DNA, which stores hereditary information. Cells can be grown in media with controlled supplies of each element. All groups start with equal numbers of identical cells and are maintained at the same temperature for the same time. Which experimental design best tests the researcher’s question?

choices.choice_text: Compare DNA production in nitrogen-free and nitrogen-containing media, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts.
choices.rationale: Wrong-element trap: Nitrogen is also a component of DNA, but this comparison tests nitrogen availability rather than phosphorus availability. Fix: Match the manipulated element to the element named in the research question.

choices.choice_text: Compare DNA production in media lacking both phosphorus and nitrogen with media containing both, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts.
choices.rationale: Confounded-variables trap: Changing phosphorus and nitrogen together prevents attributing a difference in DNA production specifically to phosphorus. Either element could limit DNA production. Fix: Change phosphorus alone while keeping nitrogen and all other elements equally available.

choices.choice_text: Compare DNA production in phosphorus-free and phosphorus-containing media, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a component of DNA, so its availability can limit production of this information-storing molecule. Changing only phosphorus availability and measuring DNA production directly tests the proposed relationship.

choices.choice_text: Compare phosphorus-free and phosphorus-containing media, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts, and measure only phosphorus remaining in each medium.
choices.rationale: Dependent-variable mismatch: Measuring phosphorus remaining describes the medium, not how much DNA the cells produce. This measurement cannot establish whether phosphorus availability limits DNA production. Fix: Measure DNA production as the response to changing phosphorus availability.

stem: Growing cells use phospholipids to build membranes and nucleic acids to store and transmit genetic information. The cells have enough of every required element except phosphorus. Which statement best explains how this shortage limits the production of these molecules?

choices.choice_text: Production of both phospholipids and nucleic acids is limited because both contain phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a required component of both phospholipids and nucleic acids. A phosphorus shortage therefore limits the cells’ ability to build membranes and produce molecules that carry genetic information.

choices.choice_text: Only nucleic acid production is limited because phospholipids do not contain phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Trap: Overlooking phosphorus in phospholipids. Phospholipids also contain phosphorus, so their production is limited by the shortage. Fix: Check the required elements in both molecule types before predicting which production is limited.

choices.choice_text: Only phospholipid production is limited because nucleic acids require nitrogen instead of phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Trap: Treating nitrogen and phosphorus requirements as mutually exclusive. Nucleic acids contain both elements; having enough nitrogen does not remove their phosphorus requirement. Fix: Check whether a molecule requires multiple elements rather than choosing just one.

choices.choice_text: Neither type of molecule is affected because biological molecules require only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.rationale: Trap: Confusing the most prevalent elements with the only required elements. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are abundant in biological molecules, but phospholipids and nucleic acids also require phosphorus. Fix: Identify each molecule’s required elements, not just the most abundant elements in living systems.

topic_title: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding
stem: A runner's working muscles release heat into surrounding tissues. The tissues' high water content helps prevent a rapid temperature increase. Which explanation links water's molecular structure to this temperature stability?

choices.choice_text: Water's uneven charge distribution enables hydrogen bonding between molecules; disrupting these attractions requires energy, resulting in a high specific heat capacity.
choices.rationale: Polar water molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another. Some incoming heat disrupts these attractions rather than increasing molecular motion, so substantial energy is needed to raise water's temperature. This helps water-rich tissues resist rapid warming.

choices.choice_text: Water absorbs heat by breaking the covalent bonds connecting oxygen and hydrogen within its molecules, resulting in a high specific heat capacity.
choices.rationale: Bond-type confusion: This explanation assigns heat absorption to bonds inside individual water molecules instead of attractions between molecules. Normal tissue warming does not split water's O–H covalent bonds. Fix: Identify whether the relevant bonds connect separate molecules or atoms within one molecule.

choices.choice_text: Water's nonpolar structure prevents attractions between its molecules, allowing tissues to absorb heat without warming rapidly.
choices.rationale: Polarity misconception: Water has an uneven charge distribution that permits hydrogen bonding between molecules. These intermolecular attractions help explain its high specific heat capacity; an absence of attractions does not. Fix: Mark water's partially positive and partially negative regions before predicting intermolecular attractions.

choices.choice_text: Water's low specific heat capacity means that a large heat input produces only a small temperature increase in tissues.
choices.rationale: Specific-heat reversal: Low specific heat capacity would allow a given heat input to produce a larger temperature increase for the same mass. Resistance to warming instead reflects high specific heat capacity. Fix: Compare temperature increases for equal masses receiving equal heat inputs.

stem: A laboratory designs two proteins for a coating that holds a dye. Each protein is a single polypeptide containing 60 amino acids. Their sequences differ at four positions, where the amino acids have different R-group properties. Tests reveal different three-dimensional shapes and weaker dye binding by one protein. Which explanation best connects the sequence differences to the binding results?

choices.choice_text: Equal chain lengths establish identical primary structures, so amino acid sequences cannot account for the unequal dye binding.
choices.rationale: The same-length-means-same-sequence trap confuses amino acid count with amino acid sequence. These proteins have different primary structures because their amino acid identities differ at four positions. Fix: Compare the amino acids at corresponding positions rather than counting them.

choices.choice_text: Peptide bonds alone control each protein’s folded shape, so differences in R groups cannot account for the unequal dye binding.
choices.rationale: The peptide-bonds-only trap overlooks interactions that shape a protein beyond linking its amino acids. R-group interactions help establish the folded shape needed for effective binding. Fix: Identify how different R-group properties could change interactions during folding.

choices.choice_text: The different folds indicate different quaternary structures because quaternary structure describes the overall shape of an individual polypeptide.
choices.rationale: The tertiary–quaternary confusion trap assigns a single chain’s overall fold to the wrong structural level. Tertiary structure describes that fold; quaternary structure involves multiple polypeptide chains interacting. Fix: Determine how many polypeptide chains are involved before naming the structural level.

choices.choice_text: Differences in R-group interactions can produce different folds, changing how effectively each protein binds the dye.
choices.rationale: The amino acid sequence determines which R groups can interact as a protein folds. Different interactions can alter the protein’s three-dimensional shape and therefore its ability to bind the dye.

stem:
During growth, a bacterial culture contains free monomers and polymer chains, each consisting of ten monomers connected by covalent bonds. The following measurements come from equal-sized samples of the culture.

Time (minutes) | Free monomers (millions) | Polymer chains (millions)
0 | 120 | 0
3 | 80 | 4
6 | 40 | 8

Which description correctly links the observed changes to the chemical reaction involved?

choices.choice_text: Free monomers decline while polymer chains become more numerous; dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds and releases water.
choices.rationale: Free monomers fall from 120 million to 40 million while polymer chains rise from zero to 8 million, indicating polymer formation. Dehydration synthesis joins monomers by forming covalent bonds, with water released during each joining reaction.

choices.choice_text: Free monomers decline while polymer chains become more numerous; hydrolysis forms covalent bonds and consumes water.
choices.rationale: Reaction-name reversal: the trend indicates assembly, but hydrolysis is assigned the bond-building role. Hydrolysis uses water to cleave bonds rather than join monomers. Fix: Identify whether monomers are joining or separating, then select the matching reaction name.

choices.choice_text: Free monomers decline while polymer chains become more numerous; dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds and consumes water.
choices.rationale: Water-direction reversal: polymer formation and the reaction name are identified appropriately, but water is treated as an input. Dehydration synthesis produces water as monomers join. Fix: Put water on the product side when representing dehydration synthesis.

choices.choice_text: Free monomers become more numerous while polymer chains decline; hydrolysis breaks covalent bonds and consumes water.
choices.rationale: Trend reversal: the chemistry describes breakdown, but the measured changes show assembly. The monomer count decreases by 80 million, while the chain count increases by 8 million. Fix: Mark each column’s change as an increase or decrease before interpreting the reaction.

stem: A cell breaks a long polymer into shorter chains by cleaving covalent bonds between its subunits. Which statement explains the chemical reaction responsible for this change?

choices.choice_text: Hydrolysis releases water as covalent bonds between subunits break.
choices.rationale: Water-direction reversal: this identifies bond cleavage but reverses water’s role. Hydrolysis consumes water rather than producing it. Fix: Place water on the reactant side when modeling hydrolysis.

choices.choice_text: Hydrolysis consumes water to break covalent bonds between subunits.
choices.rationale: Breaking the polymer into shorter chains requires bond cleavage. Hydrolysis uses water in this process, adding H to one newly separated end and OH to the other.

choices.choice_text: Hydrolysis consumes water to form covalent bonds between subunits.
choices.rationale: Bond-change reversal: this identifies water use but confuses bond cleavage with bond formation. Forming bonds between subunits would build a larger molecule, not break the polymer into shorter chains. Fix: Check whether the reaction joins subunits or separates them before describing the bonds.

choices.choice_text: Dehydration synthesis releases water as covalent bonds form between subunits.
choices.rationale: Synthesis–breakdown confusion: this accurately describes dehydration synthesis, but that process builds polymers. The cell is breaking an existing polymer apart, so bond formation cannot explain the change. Fix: Identify whether the molecule is being built or broken before naming the reaction.

topic_title: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding
stem:
A researcher adds equal amounts of heat to equal masses of water and liquid X during each heating interval. Neither liquid evaporates, and no heat escapes to the surroundings.

Temperature data:
Heating intervals completed | Water (°C) | Liquid X (°C)
0 | 20 | 20
1 | 21 | 25
2 | 22 | 30

Which statement best describes the temperature pattern and explains the molecular basis of water's response?

choices.choice_text: Water shows a larger temperature increase, indicating a lower specific heat capacity than liquid X.
choices.rationale: Comparison reversal: Water's temperature increases by 2°C, not 10°C. Its smaller increase under equal heating and equal mass indicates a higher specific heat capacity than liquid X. Fix: Subtract each liquid's initial temperature from its final temperature before comparing increases.

choices.choice_text: Water shows a smaller temperature increase because added energy breaks covalent bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen atoms.
choices.rationale: Bond-type confusion: This explanation substitutes bonds within water molecules for attractions between molecules. Water's high specific heat capacity involves disruption of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not breaking its O–H covalent bonds. Fix: Identify whether the bonds in your explanation connect separate molecules or atoms within one molecule.

choices.choice_text: Water shows a smaller temperature increase because some added energy disrupts hydrogen bonds between its polar molecules.
choices.rationale: Water warms by 2°C while liquid X warms by 10°C under equal heating. Water's polarity enables hydrogen bonding, and disrupting these attractions absorbs energy, contributing to its high specific heat capacity. This property helps stabilize temperatures in organisms and aquatic environments.

choices.choice_text: Water shows a smaller temperature increase because its nonpolar molecules do not form hydrogen bonds.
choices.rationale: Neutral-means-nonpolar misconception: Water has no net charge, but its charge distribution is uneven, making it polar. Its molecules form hydrogen bonds; the absence of these attractions does not explain its high specific heat capacity. Fix: Check charge distribution within a molecule rather than using net charge to determine polarity.

stem: Starch and cellulose are both carbohydrates found in plants. Which statement correctly connects their structures to their biological functions?

choices.choice_text: Starch and cellulose both contain glucose units, so both function primarily as energy-storage polysaccharides.
choices.rationale: The same-monomer, same-function trap ignores how polymer organization affects function. Sharing glucose monomers does not make cellulose an energy-storage carbohydrate; its organization supports plant cell walls. Fix: Compare each polymer’s organization and biological role instead of assigning function from its monomer alone.

choices.choice_text: Starch is a polysaccharide used for energy storage, whereas cellulose is a monosaccharide used for plant cell wall support.
choices.rationale: The monomer–polymer confusion misclassifies cellulose. Cellulose consists of many covalently linked sugar monomers, making it a polysaccharide rather than a monosaccharide. Fix: Check whether each carbohydrate is a single sugar unit or a chain of sugar units before naming its type.

choices.choice_text: Starch chains provide structural support in plant cell walls, whereas cellulose chains store glucose units for later energy use.
choices.rationale: The storage–support reversal assigns each polysaccharide the other’s role. Starch functions in energy storage, while cellulose contributes to plant cell wall support. Fix: Match each carbohydrate’s name to its biological role before connecting its polymer structure to that function.

choices.choice_text: Starch is a polysaccharide that stores glucose units for later energy use, whereas cellulose is a polysaccharide whose chains are organized to support plant cell walls.
choices.rationale: Both carbohydrates contain glucose monomers joined by covalent bonds, but their different organization supports different functions. Starch stores glucose units for later energy use, while cellulose chains form structural material in plant cell walls.

stem: Two DNA segments have the same length and the same total number of each base, but their bases occur in different orders. Which statement best explains how the biological information stored in these segments compares?

choices.choice_text: They must store the same information because they contain the same number of nucleotides.
choices.rationale: Length-only trap: This confuses the amount of DNA with its information content. Equal-length segments can have different nucleotide sequences. Fix: Compare base order rather than counting only the nucleotides.

choices.choice_text: They can store different information because information is encoded in the order of their nucleotides.
choices.rationale: DNA stores biological information in its nucleotide sequence. Different base orders can encode different information even when segment length and total base counts are identical.

choices.choice_text: They must store the same information because they contain the same total number of each base.
choices.rationale: Base-count trap: This treats base composition as equivalent to base sequence. Counting each base does not reveal the order in which the bases occur. Fix: Write out the sequences and compare the bases position by position.

choices.choice_text: They must store the same information because both have repeating sugar-phosphate backbones.
choices.rationale: Backbone-as-information trap: This assigns information storage to the repeating backbone rather than the variable base sequence. DNA segments share the same backbone components but can encode different information. Fix: Identify which nucleotide component varies along each DNA strand.

stem: One strand of a double-stranded DNA segment has the sequence 5′-ACGTTA-3′. A change replaces the second nucleotide, C, with A; all other nucleotides remain unchanged. A new DNA strand is then synthesized complementary to the altered strand. Predict the new strand’s sequence, written in the 5′→3′ direction.

choices.choice_text: 5′-TTCAAT-3′
choices.rationale: Parallel-strand trap: These bases complement the altered strand position by position, but the end labels incorrectly make the strands parallel. The aligned complementary strand must run 3′→5′ opposite the given strand. Fix: Label both strands’ ends before rewriting the complement in the requested direction.

choices.choice_text: 5′-UAACUU-3′
choices.rationale: DNA–RNA confusion: This sequence uses uracil as the complement of adenine. The new strand is DNA, which uses thymine rather than uracil. Fix: Identify whether the requested strand is DNA or RNA before choosing complementary bases.

choices.choice_text: 5′-TAACGT-3′
choices.rationale: Unchanged-template trap: This sequence complements the original strand rather than the altered strand. Replacing C with A changes the corresponding complementary base from G to T. Fix: Rewrite the altered strand first, then pair its bases and check strand direction.

choices.choice_text: 5′-TAACTT-3′
choices.rationale: The altered strand is 5′-AAGTTA-3′. A–T and C–G pairing gives 3′-TTCAAT-5′ because DNA strands are antiparallel. Reading the complementary strand from its 5′ end gives 5′-TAACTT-3′.

stem: An algae-production facility changes the nutrient mixture supplied to its cultures. The original mixture provided adequate amounts of every required element; the replacement supplies twice as much nitrogen but too little phosphorus, with all other required elements still adequate. The algae make nucleic acids for genetic information and phospholipids for membranes. After stored phosphorus is exhausted, and with no other phosphorus source, how should production of these materials compare with production before the change?

choices.choice_text: Production of both materials decreases because the phosphorus shortage restricts construction of both nucleic acids and phospholipids.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a required building material for both nucleic acids and phospholipids. Although nitrogen remains abundant, the reduced phosphorus supply prevents the algae from maintaining their previous production rates for either material.

choices.choice_text: Nucleic acid production stays at its previous rate because nitrogen is sufficient, while phospholipid production decreases because phosphorus is scarce.
choices.rationale: Nitrogen-only nucleic acid trap: This treats sufficient nitrogen as sufficient material for making nucleic acids. Their production also requires phosphorus, which is now limiting. Fix: Check for both nitrogen and phosphorus before predicting unchanged nucleic acid production.

choices.choice_text: Phospholipid production stays at its previous rate because carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are sufficient, while nucleic acid production decreases.
choices.rationale: All-lipids-are-alike trap: This overlooks the phosphorus requirement of phospholipids by treating all lipids as containing only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Those abundant elements cannot supply the missing phosphorus. Fix: Identify the lipid subtype and check its required elements.

choices.choice_text: Production of both materials stays at its previous rate because the extra nitrogen substitutes for the missing phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Element-substitution trap: This assumes an excess of one element can compensate for a shortage of another. Nitrogen cannot replace the phosphorus required in nucleic acids or phospholipids. Fix: Match each shortage to its required element rather than adding nutrient supplies together.

topic_title: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding
stem: During a sunny afternoon, a pond absorbs substantial heat, but its water temperature rises only slightly. This helps maintain a stable environment for aquatic organisms. Which explanation best accounts for the small temperature change?

choices.choice_text: Heat breaks the covalent bonds within water molecules, giving water a high specific heat capacity.
choices.rationale: Bond-type confusion: This explanation mistakes covalent bonds within water molecules for hydrogen bonds between molecules. Ordinary pond warming does not break water's O–H covalent bonds. Fix: Locate each bond within a molecule or between molecules before explaining heat absorption.

choices.choice_text: Water is nonpolar, so its molecules lack attractions to one another and absorb heat with little temperature change.
choices.rationale: Polarity misconception: Water is polar, and its partial charges enable hydrogen bonds between molecules. These attractions, not their absence, contribute to water's resistance to temperature change. Fix: Check whether water's oxygen and hydrogen regions have equal or unequal charge distributions.

choices.choice_text: Water has a low specific heat capacity, so absorbing substantial heat produces only a small temperature increase.
choices.rationale: Specific-heat reversal: A low specific heat capacity means less energy is needed for a given temperature increase. The pond's small temperature increase despite substantial heat absorption indicates high specific heat capacity. Fix: Ask whether a small temperature increase requires little or much energy per unit mass.

choices.choice_text: Water's polarity allows hydrogen bonds to form between molecules, and disrupting these interactions absorbs energy, giving water a high specific heat capacity.
choices.rationale: Water's partial charges allow hydrogen bonding between molecules. Much of the absorbed energy disrupts these interactions rather than increasing molecular motion, so water's temperature changes relatively little, stabilizing the organisms' environment.

stem: A microbiologist wonders whether the supply of phosphorus restricts how much phospholipid a soil bacterium makes for building its cell membranes. The bacterium can be grown in liquid cultures in which the quantity of every element is set by the investigator. Each culture is inoculated with the same number of cells from a single clone and incubated under identical temperature, oxygen, and timing conditions. Which procedure is best aligned with the microbiologist's question?

choices.choice_text: Grow cultures with low phosphorus and with ample phosphorus, supply every other element equally and adequately, and measure the amount of phospholipid the cells produce.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a building block of phospholipids, so a shortage could cap membrane-lipid synthesis. Varying only phosphorus makes it the single independent variable, and measuring phospholipid produced is the dependent variable the question asks about.

choices.choice_text: Grow cultures with low carbon and with ample carbon, supply every other element equally and adequately, and measure the amount of phospholipid the cells produce.
choices.rationale: Wrong-element trap: carbon is also in phospholipids, so it seems a reasonable variable, but this tests carbon supply rather than phosphorus supply. The results cannot answer a question about phosphorus. Fix: Check that the element you manipulate is the one named in the question.

choices.choice_text: Grow cultures low in both phosphorus and carbon and cultures ample in both, supply every other element equally and adequately, and measure the amount of phospholipid the cells produce.
choices.rationale: Confounded-variables trap: changing phosphorus and carbon together means any drop in phospholipid could come from either element. The effect of phosphorus alone cannot be isolated. Fix: Vary phosphorus only while holding carbon and all other elements constant.

choices.choice_text: Grow cultures with low phosphorus and with ample phosphorus, supply every other element equally and adequately, and measure only how much phosphorus is left in each culture liquid.
choices.rationale: Dependent-variable mismatch: leftover phosphorus describes the growth liquid, not how much phospholipid the cells actually built. Uptake could occur without any change in membrane-lipid output. Fix: Ask whether the measured variable is the response named in the question.

stem: A researcher makes artificial vesicles enclosed by a pure phospholipid bilayer containing no proteins. Equal concentrations of four substances are added to the solution outside the vesicles. Which substance would enter the vesicles most rapidly, and what is the reason?

choices.choice_text: H₂O, because it is smaller than every other substance listed and so passes through the bilayer fastest
choices.rationale: This trap judges permeability by size alone and ignores polarity. Water is small but polar, so the hydrophobic core lets it through only in small amounts without aquaporins, much more slowly than a small nonpolar molecule. Fix: Ask whether the molecule is polar or nonpolar before considering size, since a hydrophobic interior slows polar molecules.

choices.choice_text: Glucose, because cells require it for energy, so the membrane allows it to pass readily
choices.rationale: This trap explains movement by what the cell needs rather than by molecular properties. Glucose is a large polar molecule that cannot cross the hydrophobic core in meaningful amounts, and these vesicles lack the transport proteins it would require. Fix: Explain crossing using the molecule's size, polarity, and charge, and check whether a needed transport protein is present.

choices.choice_text: O₂, because it is small and nonpolar, so it can dissolve through the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer without a protein
choices.rationale: The bilayer's hydrocarbon tails form a hydrophobic core that small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ pass through freely. Polar molecules and ions are blocked or slowed by that core, and these vesicles have no channels or carriers to help them, so O₂ crosses fastest. Quantitatively, the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation predicts each ion's permeability-weighted contribution to this result.

choices.choice_text: K⁺, because a single ion is tiny and can slip between the phospholipid molecules
choices.rationale: This trap treats a charged particle as if small size were enough. The charge makes K⁺ strongly hydrophilic, so the hydrocarbon tails block it, and with no channel proteins it essentially cannot cross. Fix: Check for a charge first; any ion needs a channel or transport protein to cross the hydrophobic interior.

stem:
A student compares three fat samples whose fatty acid chains have the same length but different numbers of carbon–carbon double bonds. The student records the following results.

Sample | Double bonds per fatty acid chain | Melting temperature (°C)
X | 0 | 60
Y | 1 | 15
Z | 2 | −5

Which statement best describes the relationship in the data and explains it using fatty acid structure?

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with higher melting temperatures because unsaturated fatty acid chains are straighter and pack more closely.
choices.rationale: Reversed-trend trap: The recorded melting temperatures decrease, rather than increase, with more double bonds. Unsaturated chains have kinks, rather than being straighter. Fix: Track melting temperature from zero to two double bonds before describing the trend.

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with lower melting temperatures because kinks in unsaturated fatty acid chains interfere with close packing.
choices.rationale: Melting temperature decreases from 60°C to −5°C as the number of double bonds increases. Double bonds introduce kinks that prevent close packing, helping explain why more unsaturated fats remain liquid at lower temperatures.

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with lower melting temperatures because double bonds make the fats hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity-confusion trap: The trend is described accurately, but unsaturation does not make these fats hydrophilic. Fats remain generally nonpolar; chain kinks explain the melting-temperature pattern. Fix: Distinguish changes in chain shape from changes in attraction to water.

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with lower melting temperatures because adding double bonds makes the fatty acid chains more saturated.
choices.rationale: Saturation-definition trap: The trend is described accurately, but adding double bonds increases unsaturation, not saturation. Saturated fatty acid chains contain only single carbon–carbon bonds. Fix: Check for carbon–carbon double bonds before classifying a fatty acid as saturated.

stem:
Researchers compare two versions of a protein that binds a target molecule. Each version consists of one intact polypeptide containing 100 amino acids. The versions differ only in the amino acid at position 40. Measurements are made under identical conditions.

Protein version | R group at position 40 | Folded shape | Protein molecules bound to target (%)
Original | Hydrophobic | Reference shape | 90
Modified | Charged | Different from reference | 20

Which statement best describes the relationship in the data and connects it to protein structure and function?

choices.choice_text: The versions have identical primary structures because they contain the same number of amino acids, so the binding difference cannot reflect a sequence change.
choices.rationale: Length–sequence confusion: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, not merely the number of amino acids. The replacement at position 40 changes that sequence despite equal chain lengths. Fix: Compare amino acid identities and order, not just chain length.

choices.choice_text: The modified protein binds fewer target molecules because replacing the R group breaks peptide bonds and shortens the polypeptide.
choices.rationale: Side-chain–backbone confusion: R groups influence folding interactions, whereas peptide bonds connect amino acids in the backbone. Both measured proteins have intact, equally long polypeptides, so chain shortening does not explain the binding decrease. Fix: Separate changes in R-group interactions from breaks in the peptide backbone.

choices.choice_text: The modified protein’s different folded shape represents a change in quaternary structure that explains its lower target binding.
choices.rationale: Tertiary–quaternary confusion: Quaternary structure involves interactions between multiple polypeptides. Each version contains only one polypeptide, so its overall three-dimensional folding concerns tertiary structure. Fix: Count polypeptide chains before identifying tertiary or quaternary structure.

choices.choice_text: The modified protein has a different folded shape and lower target binding, consistent with changed R-group interactions affecting protein function.
choices.rationale: Target binding decreases from 90% to 20% as folded shape changes. Replacing a hydrophobic R group with a charged R group can alter interactions within the protein, connecting the sequence change to altered folding and binding function.

stem: A cell in a gland secretes large amounts of a protein hormone. Electron micrographs show that its cytoplasm is packed with extensive, flattened membrane sacs whose outer surfaces are densely studded with ribosomes. Which statement best explains how this structure supports the cell's function?

choices.choice_text: The sacs are smooth ER; their extensive membranes synthesize lipids and detoxify substances, supplying the materials the cell needs to secrete the hormone.
choices.rationale: This confuses rough and smooth ER. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and carries out lipid synthesis and detoxification, so it cannot explain heavy protein production by ribosome-studded membranes. Fix: Check whether the described membranes carry ribosomes before naming the ER type, since ribosomes signal rough ER and protein synthesis.

choices.choice_text: The sacs are Golgi stacks; the ribosomes on their flattened surfaces synthesize the hormone, which is then released directly from the Golgi.
choices.rationale: This mistakes flattened sacs for the Golgi just because of their shape. The Golgi is not studded with ribosomes; it modifies and packages proteins that were already made elsewhere, so it does not synthesize the hormone. Fix: Ask which feature of the structure matches the function, and look for bound ribosomes rather than relying on sac shape alone.

choices.choice_text: The ribosomes are attached to the membranes so they can produce ATP, supplying the energy the cell needs to export large amounts of hormone.
choices.rationale: This assigns a mitochondrial job to ribosomes. Ribosomes, made of rRNA and protein, synthesize proteins from mRNA; ATP synthesis is supported by the convoluted inner mitochondrial membrane, not by ribosome-studded membranes. Fix: Match each structure to its own function first, then ask whether the feature described actually supports that function.

choices.choice_text: The sacs are rough ER; their membrane-bound ribosomes synthesize the protein hormone, and the ER membranes, as part of the endomembrane system, carry the protein onward to be modified, packaged, and transported out of the cell.
choices.rationale: This names the structure (rough ER), the function (protein synthesis), and the feature that makes it possible: ribosomes bound to the ER membrane. An extensive rough ER means many ribosomes making protein, and its membranes feed the endomembrane pathway that modifies, packages, and transports the hormone for secretion.

stem: A change in a mammal’s diet increases the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in its stored fats. The total mass of stored fat and the lengths of the fatty acid chains remain unchanged. At the same temperature, which prediction best connects the structural change to the properties and function of the stored fats?

choices.choice_text: The stored fats will tend to be less liquid while continuing to serve as a long-term energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Reversed packing effect: This prediction treats double bonds as promoting tighter packing. Their kinks instead reduce close packing, so increased unsaturation favors a more liquid state at the same temperature. Fix: Trace double bonds → kinks → reduced packing before predicting physical state.

choices.choice_text: The stored fats will tend to be more liquid and become water-soluble, preventing them from serving as an energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Liquid–soluble confusion: A more liquid state does not mean greater water solubility. Increasing unsaturation does not make fats hydrophilic or remove their energy-storage function. Fix: Evaluate physical state and water solubility separately.

choices.choice_text: The stored fats will tend to be more liquid and form phospholipid bilayers instead of serving as an energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Lipid-class interchangeability: This prediction assigns the membrane-forming role of phospholipids to fats. Altering fatty acid unsaturation does not convert stored fats into phospholipids. Fix: Identify the lipid class before assigning its biological function.

choices.choice_text: The stored fats will tend to be more liquid while continuing to serve as a long-term energy reserve.
choices.rationale: Unsaturated fatty acids contain carbon–carbon double bonds that introduce kinks, reducing close packing and favoring a more liquid state. Changing the degree of unsaturation does not eliminate the energy-storage function of fats.

stem: A researcher redesigns a double-stranded DNA identification tag to distinguish two sample batches. The strand used to build the redesigned tag originally reads 5′-TGCATGAC-3′; the researcher substitutes A for the sixth nucleotide, G, leaving every other position unchanged. Predict the sequence of a DNA strand synthesized complementary to the redesigned strand, reported in the 5′→3′ direction.

choices.choice_text: 5′-ACGTATTG-3′
choices.rationale: Parallel-strand trap: The base matches are appropriate, but the end labels place both aligned strands in the same direction. Opposite the redesigned strand, this complementary sequence must be labeled 3′-ACGTATTG-5′. Fix: Mark opposite ends on the aligned strands, then read the complement from 5′.

choices.choice_text: 5′-GUUAUGCA-3′
choices.rationale: DNA–RNA confusion: Using U opposite A applies RNA base pairing to a requested DNA strand. DNA contains thymine, not uracil. Fix: Identify the requested nucleic acid before selecting T or U.

choices.choice_text: 5′-GTTATGCA-3′
choices.rationale: The redesigned strand reads 5′-TGCATAAC-3′. Complementary base pairing and antiparallel orientation produce an aligned strand of 3′-ACGTATTG-5′. Reversing the order to report that strand 5′→3′ gives 5′-GTTATGCA-3′.

choices.choice_text: 5′-GTCATGCA-3′
choices.rationale: Unchanged-template trap: This sequence is complementary to the tag before redesign. The G-to-A substitution requires a corresponding C-to-T change in the newly synthesized complement. Fix: Write the redesigned sequence before constructing and orienting its complement.

stem:
A researcher tracks polymers and free monomers in a reaction mixture. Each polymer contains six monomers joined by covalent bonds.

Time (minutes) | Number of polymers | Number of free monomers
0 | 10 | 0
5 | 5 | 30
10 | 0 | 60

Which statement best describes the trend in the data and the reaction responsible?

choices.choice_text: Polymers decrease as free monomers increase; dehydration synthesis releases water to break covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: Reaction-name reversal: this identifies breakdown but assigns it to dehydration synthesis. Dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds between monomers rather than breaking those bonds. Fix: Determine whether bonds are forming or breaking before naming the reaction.

choices.choice_text: Polymers decrease as free monomers increase; hydrolysis releases water when it breaks covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: Water-direction reversal: this correctly identifies hydrolysis but treats water as a product. Hydrolysis consumes water during bond cleavage. Fix: Place water on the reactant side when describing hydrolysis.

choices.choice_text: Polymers increase as free monomers decrease; dehydration synthesis releases water to form covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: Trend reversal: this describes polymer formation, but the table shows polymers decreasing from 10 to 0 and free monomers increasing from 0 to 60. Fix: Compare each column’s final value with its initial value before identifying the reaction.

choices.choice_text: Polymers decrease as free monomers increase; hydrolysis consumes water to break covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: The decrease in polymers and increase in free monomers indicate polymer breakdown. Hydrolysis breaks the bonds between monomers by adding water, supplying H to one resulting end and OH to the other.

stem: A protein consists of a single polypeptide chain. In a second version of the protein, one amino acid with a hydrophobic R group is replaced by an amino acid with a charged R group. The second version folds differently and functions less effectively. Which explanation best connects the amino acid replacement to these observations?

choices.choice_text: The two versions have identical primary structures because they contain the same number of amino acids, so sequence cannot explain the functional difference.
choices.rationale: This is the same-length-means-same-sequence trap. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, so replacing one amino acid changes primary structure even when chain length stays constant. Fix: Compare amino acid identities and order, not just chain length.

choices.choice_text: Only peptide bonds determine the protein’s folded shape, so changing an R group cannot explain the functional difference.
choices.rationale: This is the peptide-bonds-only trap. Peptide bonds link amino acids, but interactions involving R groups also help determine the folded shape and therefore protein function. Fix: Trace how the changed R group could alter interactions within the protein.

choices.choice_text: The replacement changes quaternary structure because quaternary structure describes how a single polypeptide folds into its functional shape.
choices.rationale: This is the tertiary–quaternary confusion trap. Quaternary structure involves interactions between multiple polypeptides; the overall three-dimensional fold of this single chain is its tertiary structure. Fix: Count the polypeptide chains before identifying tertiary or quaternary structure.

choices.choice_text: The replacement changes R-group interactions, which can alter the protein’s three-dimensional shape and function.
choices.rationale: R-group interactions help determine a protein’s tertiary structure. Changing an R group can change these interactions and the resulting fold, affecting the protein’s ability to function.

stem: Researchers study a mutant plant that cannot synthesize cellulose. Its cells form weak cell walls, and the plant cannot hold its stem upright. Which statement best explains this observation?

choices.choice_text: Cellulose is a polysaccharide of glucose monomers covalently linked into long linear chains that give plant cell walls structural support.
choices.rationale: Cellulose is a carbohydrate polymer built from glucose monomers. Its function is structural, not energy storage. Its long linear chains reinforce the cell wall, so a plant that cannot make cellulose has weak walls and cannot support its stem.

choices.choice_text: Cellulose is the main energy-storage polysaccharide in plants, so without it the cells lack the fuel needed to grow upright.
choices.rationale: This trap assumes every carbohydrate exists for energy and confuses cellulose with starch, the plant storage polysaccharide. The observation is a structural failure in the wall, not an energy shortage. Fix: Ask whether the observed defect is structural or energetic before choosing a polysaccharide's function.

choices.choice_text: Cellulose is a monosaccharide that plant cells break down for quick energy, so the cells cannot fuel cell wall construction.
choices.rationale: This confuses monomer with polymer. Cellulose is a polysaccharide made of many glucose monomers, and it serves as a wall component rather than a quick energy source. Fix: Check whether a carbohydrate is a single sugar unit or a chain of many units.

choices.choice_text: Cellulose is a protein whose folded amino acid chains form fibers, so without it the wall loses its folded protein framework.
choices.rationale: This misclassifies cellulose as a protein because it forms fibers. Cellulose is a carbohydrate made of glucose monomers, not amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Fix: Identify the monomer first: sugars build carbohydrates, amino acids build proteins.
